title: Before sleep
hook: a traditional Jewish bedtime prayer begins by forgiving anyone who hurt you that day

segments.voice: Yesterday, letting the story change, and Naomi's story told twice. Your line was a new telling. Which version did you carry? Today, a practice for the end of every day, before the stories pile up. Day nine hundred ninety-two.

What does the mind do in the last minutes before sleep? Lights off, phone down, and the day starts replaying. The comment in the meeting. The text that was a little too short. The friend who didn't ask how it went. Small things, mostly. But small things left overnight have a way of being bigger by morning, and bigger still by the end of the week. A Jewish tradition has an answer that's built into bedtime itself. Before the Shema is said at night, a prayer comes first, and it opens with forgiveness.
screen: `LIGHTS OFF. THE DAY REPLAYS.` → `SMALL THINGS GROW OVERNIGHT.` → `A PRAYER AT THE BEDSIDE.`

segments.voice: First, where it sits. The bedtime Shema is a set of prayers said at night, at home, often in bed. In the traditional prayer book, before the Shema itself, there is a short passage addressed to the Master of the world. Second, what it says. In paraphrase: I hereby forgive anyone who angered me or wronged me, whether against my body, my property or my honor, whether by accident or on purpose, in word or in deed. It doesn't ask who deserves it, and it isn't limited to today. It covers the whole list in one sweep. Third, the line that surprises people. The prayer goes further than forgiving. It asks that no one be punished on my account. Not just: I let it go. But: I don't want them to suffer because of what they did to me. That's a big request to make about someone who was rude to you at lunch. And it's said at night, before sleep, when the day's grudges are still fresh. Fourth, a neighbor. Christians read a line from the letter to the Ephesians that points at the same hour: "Be ye angry, and sin not: let not the sun go down upon your wrath." Two traditions, each with its own words, both asking that the day's anger be set down at the edge of night. The idea is simple and practical. Clear the small debts daily, the way you'd wash the dishes before bed, so you don't wake up to a sink full of them.
screen: `A PRAYER BEFORE THE SHEMA.` · `BODY, PROPERTY, HONOR.` · `LET NO ONE BE PUNISHED FOR ME.` · `NOT THE SUN ON YOUR WRATH.` · then, large: `I FORGIVE TODAY.`

segments.voice: Whatever time it is now, sit as if it were the end of the day. Let the breath slow. Run back through today, or yesterday if it's morning, like flipping through photos. Stop at each small sting: a word, a look, a delay, a silence. For each one, don't argue the case. Just say, silently, your line: I forgive today. Then move on to the next. If something is too big for tonight, set it aside; this practice is for the small ones. If you pray, you can use the words of a traditional bedtime prayer from your own tradition. The bell holds the time.
Before sleep. The last minutes of the day, when a Jewish bedtime prayer forgives the day's wrongs before the Shema is said. Today's word.
Your line: I forgive today. Tonight, before you sleep, flip through the day once more and say it to each small sting. Day nine hundred ninety-two.

howItsDone: Jews who say the bedtime Shema (Kriat Shema al ha-Mitah) begin, in the traditional prayer book, with a passage forgiving anyone who wronged them, before saying the Shema.

original.note: Hebrew: I hereby forgive. Words from the forgiveness passage before the bedtime Shema.

trapdoor: what you thought: a bedtime prayer is about asking for a good night.
what it means: this one starts by forgiving the whole day's wrongs, before sleep.
what a scholar hears: the passage forgives, then asks that no one be punished on my account, which is a step past letting go.

notes: The forgiveness passage before the bedtime Shema (Ribbono shel olam, hareini mochel…) is paraphrased; confirm the paraphrase (body, property, honor; accident or on purpose; word or deed; no one punished on my account) against a standard siddur.
Hebrew הֲרֵינִי מוֹחֵל: confirm pointing; the passage begins Ribbono shel olam, and these words follow.
'often in bed' and 'said at night, at home': confirm wording.
Ephesians 4:26 is introduced as a neighbor sharing the theme, not a comparison.
Editor pass: Ephesians 4:26 speaks of anger, not forgiveness, so the comparison line now says both set the day's anger down before night.

Audit pass: the prayer forgives any wrong, not only that day's (it adds 'whether in this incarnation or another'), so howItsDone and the teach no longer limit it to the day. Many siddurim word it as forgiving 'every person of Israel' (kol bar Yisrael), others 'every person'; the paraphrase says 'anyone', so a Keeper should confirm. 'Paul's letter to the Ephesians' changed to 'the letter to the Ephesians', since its authorship is debated. Review updated to day 991's new Ruth story.
